 RBI quietly effects another rate hike via tighter liquidity to counter crude surge and rupee fall
 RBI quietly effects another rate hike via tighter liquidity to counter crude surge and rupee fall
 The reason for the tightness is an obvious fall in liquidity due to a mix of factors: dollar sales by RBI along with GST payment outflows around Oct 20 plus cash withdrawals which are typical during the festive season. 
 Latha Venkatesh 
 October 27, 2026 / 12:40 IST Share --> 
 --> 
 --> 
 --> 
 Reserve Bank of India 
 The RBI appears to have quietly effected yet another rate hike of 25 bps, through tighter liquidity. That's what one can conclude looking at the sharp increase in market yields for the past 2 weeks, to be precise since October 14. The key policy rate WACR or the weighted average call rate jumped from 5.31% on Oct 13, to 5.52% on Oct 14 and 5.75% on Oct 15. Call rates dipped a bit over the weekend on Oct 16 and 17, but from Oct 19 onwards were back up at 5.7%.
 Nor was call market the only one to see such a surge in yields. Sample this table:
 Instrument Yield on Oct 14 (%) Yield on Oct 27 (%) Rise in bps 
 1-year CD 7.5 8.1 60bps 
 1 year NBFC CPs 7.85 8.4 55bps 
 1-year OIS 6.35 6.66 31bps 
 6-month OIS 6.0 6.36 36bps 
 The reason for the tightness is an obvious fall in liquidity due to a mix of factors: dollar sales by RBI along with GST payment outflows around Oct 20 plus cash withdrawals which are typical during the festive season. The point to note is RBI did not replenish the liquidity fully. It did do five variable rate repo auctions to supply liquidity to the market, but in each case it gave less liquidity than the market sought :
 Date VRR Length Notified Amount (Rs cr) Bid Received For (Rs cr) 
 Oct 19 7-day  1,00,000 1,50,000 
 Oct 21 Overnight 50,000 93,251 
 Oct 22 Overnight 50,000 1,62,000 
 Oct 23 3-day 50,000 1,06,000 
 Oct 26 4-day 1,50,000 1,86,000 
 Related Stories
 India's overseas investment commitments fall 37% to $4.34 billion in September 
 Rupee opens flat at 95.19 against the dollar as traders eye crude oil, Fed decision 
 Currency Check | Rupee opens with marginal gains at 95.16 per dollar; Asian peers mixed 
 Clearly the wanton lower-than-required repo auction, led to the higher call rate and other yields.
 Importantly the rise in market yields could not have been because of the sentiment impact of the rise in US yields. US 10-year yields peaked on Oct 6 at 5.36% and by Oct 14 had receded to 5.1% and then to below 5%. Yes, crude prices were a sentiment dampener on bond prices. Brent crude which was hugging the $100-mark from mid September to mid-October, started rising from $105 /bl on Oct 14 to hit $116 on Oct 26.
 But one must not ignore the signs emanating from RBI’s action. Under the inflation targeting framework the RBI is bound to keep the call rate at the policy repo rate which was hiked to 5.5% from 5.25% on Oct 7. Accordingly the call rate did rise from 5.16% till Oct 6 to 5.36% starting Oct 7, after the rate hike. But it didn’t touch 5.5% till Oct 14 and has since prevailed closer to 5.7%, effectively reflecting a 50 bps repo rate hike by the RBI.
 One way to interpret this surge in call rate is to see it as a stealth rate hike to defend the rupee. The RBI tried to quell the rupee with its hawkish policy on Oct 7 which included a rate hike and an unexpected change in stance to “calibrated tightening” from “neutral”. When the rupee fell sharply on Oct 8 and 9, the RBI announced a clutch of steps on Oct 10 to suck out short sellers and excessive hedging by importers.
 Thereafter from Oct 14, it quietly unleashed its liquidity steps too. On hindsight one can see two warnings. In his interview to Moneycontrol on October 14, the governor said “:We normally do not use monetary policy to address financial stability risks. We follow the separation principle – monetary policy for price stability and targeted regulatory, supervisory and macroprudential tools for financial stability reasons, but they cannot be separated completely. It is important to keep in mind that monetary policy can have a bearing on financial stability. Therefore, monetary policy has to keep financial stability in mind while taking decisions and can also be used for this too.”
 If one interprets financial stability here as rupee, then the RBI’s actions fit perfectly. There was yet another hint in the “Liquidity Conditions” chapter in the MPR (Monetary Policy Review ) released along with the policy. The last sentence of that chapter says : “Going ahead, liquidity management operations will be conditional on evolving domestic financial conditions, monetary policy decisions and the stance of monetary policy.”
 This statement clearly shows what the RBI actually meant by calibrated tightening. In a neutral stance, the WACR ( weighted average call rate) largely stays at the repo rate. But in a situation of calibrated tightening, RBI is hinting it can keep the call rate at the upper end of the range between the SDF(5.25%) and the MSF rate(5.75%).
 Effectively the RBI has raised policy rates by 50 bps, likely responding to both the possible sharp rise in inflation (with crude staying at $115) and the need to stabilise the rupee.
 Latha Venkatesh is Executive Editor of CNBC-TV18
